The sharp rise in monthly statistics for July, when set against the equivalent period in 2025, highlights Vladimir Putin 's ever more belligerent military stance. This may include adverts from us and 3rd parties based on our understanding. You can unsubscribe at any time. Read our Privacy Policy "The numbers do not lie," stated a post by NATO's Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum. "Compare July 2025 with July 2026, and the picture becomes clear: scrambles on NATO's eastern flank increased by more than 250%. The reason? Russian military aircraft repeatedly flew close to NATO airspace without a flight plan and transponder signal, leaving our fighters to launch, intercept, and identify them. Every scramble proves that we are alert. Every interception proves that NATO airspace is protected." In a separate development on August 3, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft roughly 37 miles north of Leba in the Baltic Sea. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Chilling map exposes incoming Russia army attacks on Ukraine Huge blow for Putin as Ukraine's Zelensky hails major breakthrough That very same day, two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons took off from Šiauliai, Lithuania, responding to direct instructions from NATO's Combined Air Operations Center, to intercept two Russian military aircraft flying over the Baltic. The aircraft types were not disclosed, and both stayed within international airspace. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT While Russian aircraft generally steer clear of entering NATO airspace directly, alliance jets have been scrambled on numerous occasions in response to Putin's drone violations over Romania. On August 2, alliance warplanes were dispatched after a Russian drone breached NATO airspace over Romania for 20 minutes. Ukraine brought down the aircraft after it left Romanian territory. The incident highlighted Moscow's contempt for clear Western warnings to halt its kamikaze drone incursions. This represented the fourth time in ten days that a Russian Shahed drone had encroached upon Romanian airspace. The aftermath of a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia (Image: social media/east2west news) Three were destroyed by scrambled Romanian F-16 fighters on 24, 25 and 26 July. Subsequently, on 30 July, NATO sent fighter jets over Poland after a nuclear-capable Kh-101 missile breached Polish airspace by nearly 60 miles before coming down in a field in the Lublin region. In another incident, a NATO Saab JAS 39 Gripen supersonic multirole fighter was photographed intercepting a Russian Aerospace Forces Tu-22M3 bomber as it travelled over the Baltic Sea on 21 July. The photograph was taken from the Russian nuclear-capable aircraft. Fears are growing that the Ukrainian conflict could escalate as provocations increase, potentially dragging NATO members into direct combat. NATO's unease over Russian probes heightened as Moscow today claimed to have shot down more than 600 Ukrainian drones. Despite these assertions, Kyiv drones set ablaze one of Russia 's biggest oil refineries - Slavneft-YANOS in Yaroslavl, 155 miles northeast of Moscow, sparking multiple distinct fires throughout the site. Thick smoke billowed into the sky from the complex, which is critical for oil deliveries to the Russian military and the capital. The strike was part of Ukraine's strategy to undermine Putin's oil economy which bankrolls his war. https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage's Reform UK has promised to use its first 100 days in government to ditch a string of policy costs from energy bills, a move the party claims would save people £250 per year. The announcement will be made by Reform’s Deputy Leader Richard Tice in a speech at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham on Friday. The proposal would reduce costs for voters partly by scrapping levies already directly applied to household bills and partly by reducing costs for gas generators, savings which the party says will be passed on to consumers. Advertisement Advertisement The cost of energy “represents a national crisis,” Tice said. A cap on energy costs, expressed as the average household's bill and set every quarter by the Ofgem regulator, is set to jump 4 percent next month. The hike is principally driven by the impact of the Middle East conflict on global gas markets. In a statement, Reform said it will remove charges levied on gas generators, including through the U.K. Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS). The ETS is designed to force down harmful greenhouse gas emissions by the most energy-intensive manufacturers. The Labour government has made attempts to link emissions trading systems in London and Brussels central to ongoing “reset” talks between the U.K. and EU, arguing that will cut industrial costs and ease trade barriers. Both sides are targeting a deal at the next EU- U.K. summit, expected this fall. Tice will also pledge to scrap Carbon Price Support (CPS), a tax on power generators introduced by former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron. The Labour government under Keir Starmer had already pledged to remove CPS costs from bills from 2028 . The party said removing those two levies would shave £90 per year from energy bills. Reform pledged to scrap other policy costs currently added to household bills, including the remainder of the Renewables Obligation scheme, used to fund legacy net-zero projects. The majority of levies associated with the scheme were shifted into general taxation by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves last year. Advertisement Advertisement Removing that cost, as well as charges to pay for the so-called Feed-in Tariff, used to encourage take-up of renewables, and for the Warm Home Discount, which funds help with electricity costs for struggling households, would save another £80, the party said. Reform said it would also make permanent Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s decision to scrap VAT on household electricity bills, a policy the government has forecast will cost £850 million over the next year. Farage's party said it would also remove VAT on gas. Tice pledged Reform would “take extraordinary measures to bring costs down, restore fairness to the energy sector, and take urgent action within 100 days of taking office to put an extra £250 a year back into your pockets.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Despite the Maryland incident, beavers rarely get rabies. Photograph: Troy Harrison/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Despite the Maryland incident, beavers rarely get rabies. Photograph: Troy Harrison/Getty Images US news Rabies concerns grow in the US – but it’s unclear if there’s an increase of the fatal disease Rabid goats at a North Carolina petting zoo and a diseased beaver attacking a Maryland boy have set the public on edge Eric Berger Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Recent unusual incidents involving humans and rabid animals and a subsequent Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advisory have prompted concerns about rabies, but it’s not clear if there has actually been an increase in cases of the deadly disease in the United States, experts say. In recent months, rabid beavers have attacked three people in Maryland , and hundreds of people were exposed to goats with rabies at a petting zoo in North Carolina , according to news reports. The CDC issued a health advisory on 10 September “in response to recent reports of increases in human exposures to rabid or possibly rabid animals”. Despite the uncertainty over whether people encountered rabid animals or simply were worried that they did, the increased news coverage and greater awareness of the disease is a good thing, experts suggested. Man dies of rabies after kidney transplant from donor who saved kitten from skunk Read more “Any time that the subject gets good coverage and people can learn a little bit about how they can be safe, I think that is a win for public health,” said Zak Mertz, CEO of the New England Wildlife Center. Hundreds of people used to die annually in the United States from rabies, but measures like vaccines and animal control programs have led to fewer than 10 people typically dying each year from the diseases, according to the CDC . Still, from July to August, the federal agency received 17% more rabies-related inquiries, including reports of mass exposure events, as compared with the same period last year. The agency also received reports from state health departments of increased administration of post-exposure prophylaxis treatments after a possible rabies exposure. In July, a wild skunk entered a baby goats’ pen at a farm in Harmony, North Carolina, CNN reported . Months later, hundreds of people interacted with the goats, at least some of which had rabies. Local health departments then monitored those humans, and hundreds received prophylaxis treatment. There have not been reports of any related deaths. In Maryland, a 13-year-old was swimming at a state park when a beaver attacked him. The boy survived but had to have three surgeries to his chest and hands to repair nerve damage. When asked if there was a common cause for such incidents, Meghan Davis, an associate professor of environmental health and engineering at Johns Hopkins University said: “I think what we are seeing is a little bit of bad luck.” The goats had not been old enough to be vaccinated. Beavers rarely get rabies. Despite all the scientific advancements, people do still occasionally die from rabies. In 2011, Tonji Durant’s sister, Ivy, called her local animal control office in South Carolina to inform them of bats in her home. The local officials did not provide her with guidance on what she should do to protect herself, such as getting a medical assessment, Durant, a retired CDC epidemiologist, said. Months later, she developed flu-like symptoms, Durant said. Only then did providers administer a rabies test, which came back positive, but after symptoms develop, there is little doctors can do. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “The older you get, the more you miss your siblings,” said Durant, who thinks her sister’s death was preventable. “Communication is really critical. Clinicians working with state and local health departments; communities working with state and local health departments.” If a person is worried that they potentially had contact with a rabid animal, they should contact the state or their healthcare provider, Mertz said. Those who have been bitten by a potentially rabid animal should wash the wound thoroughly and immediately seek medical attention, Davis said. “Don’t wait; seek help,” she said. It’s also important for people to ensure that their pets’ vaccinations are up to date. “Because [rabies] has largely been under control,” Davis said, “it doesn’t always reach the public eye.” Explore more on these topics US news Infectious diseases Maryland North Carolina Health news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: A police checkpoint near RAF Fairford after a major incident was declared on Sunday. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA View image in fullscreen A police checkpoint near RAF Fairford after a major incident was declared on Sunday. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA UK security and counter-terrorism Analysis Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west but its track record has been mixed Mon 28 Sep 2026 17.36 EDT First published on Mon 28 Sep 2026 13.52 EDT Share Investigators may be some way from determining exactly what led five men with three vans to a village just outside RAF Fairford in the small hours of Sunday – but the fact they have all been released on bail without immediate charge suggests they are not deemed to pose a serious and violent threat. In a moment where wider geopolitical tensions mean external threats are perceived to be close, the question of whether Iran had a hand in the alleged plot remains open. Nonetheless, the bailing of the men is a mercifully lower-key development in an investigation that appeared of the utmost gravity. Farmer who alerted police to RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot says there was ‘no follow-up’ Read more Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform, had earlier insisted that the Fairford incident “proves my point on Iran” and argued that anybody arriving on small boats should not be allowed to move around in the UK. The latter point was an irrelevant argument, already weakened when police said at lunchtime that all five were UK nationals from London. Though the five were arrested on suspicion of carrying explosives and involvement in a terror plot, after more than 24 hours of searches, nothing had been discovered that would prompt further police action – perhaps explaining why MI5 had no idea that the men and their vans would turn up a mile from the base with unclear intent. View image in fullscreen A US bomber and armoured car at RAF Fairford. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian British officials admitted on Sunday the arrests were not led by intelligence, but rather last-minute warnings on the ground. Counter-terror police said they were first aware of three vehicles travelling to the base at 12.45am on Sunday, while a local farmer phoned 999 at 1.36am after the vans blocked the entrance to her drive . The next day Trump made a characteristically inflated claim that the US and UK had been monitoring the men for “a long time” and that they had been trying to do “big damage”. Threat levels at Fairford have been at the highest level for several days, apparently backing this up – but UK sources say this was related to wider concerns about threats to US bases, not specific to the site. RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers, essentially an American base on British soil. It has been used by the US in its bombing campaign against Iran, after the former prime minister Keir Starmer agreed to allow American strikes on Iranian missile launch sites in the war Donald Trump started in the spring. The base has also been a source of explicit interest to Tehran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement on 23 July, as the US carried out a 13th day of consecutive bombing attacks. It said that any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets” . That would give Fairford an obvious value, though it is not clear why anyone from London would feel bold enough to attack a military base, given it would be expected to be protected by armed personnel. Rational plotters probably would not expect to survive, and would at least expect the most serious penalties available under law. When the suspects’ release was announced, there was no firm information from UK counter-terror police about what explosives were found or whether there was deemed to be viable devices in the vans – the kind of information that would immediately point to the degree of intent in any terror plot. Subsequently, it emerged no explosive material had been found. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Tehran has been trying to step up attacks on targets in the west over the past three years, as fighting in the Middle East has sprawled and expanded after October 2023, and particularly after Trump joined Israel to start a full-scale war on Iran in February. But while its propagandists make heavy threats about British military bases online, Iran’s actual threat is mixed. A year ago, Ken McCallum, the head of MI5, said the Security Service had “tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots in just the one year”. Two Romanian men were found guilty in July of stabbing the Iranian journalist Pouria Zeraati in the leg in Wimbledon two years earlier in a state-directed attack; he worked for the independent Persian channel Iran International. Yvette Cooper, then home secretary, sanctioned an IRGC-backed terror group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, in July after it claimed responsibility for a series of attacks in the UK, including the burning of four Jewish community ambulances in March. But while four men have pleaded guilty, evidence in the case has yet to be heard in court, with prosecutors only saying so far there was a “terrorist connection” . In April police closed and searched part of Kensington Gardens near the Israeli embassy in London after an online video appeared to suggest the building had been targeted by drones containing hazardous substances. On that occasion, nothing was found.
